texts.label: A
texts.title: The planner
texts.text: Urban trees are infrastructure. They lower summer temperatures and interrupt rainwater as effectively as some engineered systems. Treating them as decoration makes their maintenance seem optional, when in fact it is part of managing a city.

texts.label: B
texts.title: The ecologist
texts.text: The strongest case for trees is not their convenience to humans. A street can support insects, birds and fungi if planting is diverse and connected. The ecological benefits are easily lost when every tree is selected for appearance alone.

texts.label: C
texts.title: The resident
texts.text: I support more trees, but I dislike schemes that ignore the people who live beside them. Roots can damage pavements and dense shade can make a narrow street feel unsafe. Consultation should shape planting rather than follow it.

texts.label: D
texts.title: The economist
texts.text: The benefits of trees are real, though difficult to distribute evenly. A new park may raise nearby property values and push out the residents it was intended to help. Greening policy therefore needs measures that protect affordability.

questions.prompt: Who argues that trees should be managed as a fundamental city service?
questions.explanation: The planner calls trees infrastructure and links them to city management.

questions.prompt: Who is most concerned with species variety?
questions.explanation: The ecologist recommends diverse and connected planting for wildlife.

questions.prompt: Who insists that local people should influence decisions?
questions.explanation: The resident says consultation should shape planting.

questions.prompt: Who warns that an environmental improvement can have an unintended social cost?
questions.explanation: The economist links parks with rising property values and displacement.
